title: Boundary limits of the matrix geometric mean and the failure of unrestricted GLT closure
shortTitle: Same symbols in, symbol 4/5 out: when the geometric mean of GLT matrix-sequences breaks
oneLine: Every value the matrix geometric mean can approach near a singular pair is described by one rank condition, and the same mechanism gives bounded positive definite GLT sequences with identical symbols whose geometric means have symbol 4/5 instead of 1 on half the interval, refuting a published theorem; the formula is safe exactly when the symbols share no zero region or never overlap.
abstract: The geometric mean A#B of two positive definite matrices is the matrix analogue of √(ab), used to average covariance and structured matrices and to define the Matsumoto fidelity of quantum states. It is continuous on positive definite pairs but not at singular ones. This candidate proves that X is a limit of A_j#B_j with positive definite A_j → A and B_j → B exactly when X ⪰ 0, the block matrix [[A, X], [X, B]] is positive semidefinite and its rank is at most the dimension N; a dilation description with an auxiliary contraction already follows from recent work of Jones, and the explicit elimination is the contribution. At equal inputs this gives the full set of limits and the exact interval of limiting Matsumoto fidelities. For generalized locally Toeplitz (GLT) matrix-sequences it constructs uniformly bounded positive definite inputs with identical scalar symbols whose geometric means have symbol 4/5 times the predicted one, or no eigenvalue distribution at all. These refute Theorem 4 and Conjecture 1 of the arXiv version of Ilyas, Khan, Loi and Serra-Capizzano and, according to an AI-assisted reading of the published text, Theorem 3 and Conjecture 1 of their 2025 article in Linear Algebra and its Applications; the failing proof step is located. On the positive side, closure holds for every Kubo–Ando mean when the sum of the symbols is positive definite almost everywhere; the regularised symbol is always an upper envelope for the eigenvalues of the means; and for bounded Riemann-integrable scalar symbols of the space variable only, the formula holds for every realisation if and only if the symbols have no common zero set of positive measure or essentially disjoint supports. The classical discontinuity, Ando's maximal characterisation and the envelope X ⪯ A#B are earlier work. AI-assisted, unrefereed candidate; no external peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification is claimed.

keyResults: Rank criterion (Theorem 1, proof): X is a limit of A_j#B_j with positive definite A_j → A, B_j → B exactly when X ⪰ 0, [[A, X], [X, B]] ⪰ 0 and rank [[A, X], [X, B]] ≤ N; every limit lies below the regularised mean A#B.

Equal inputs and fidelity (Corollaries 2-3, proof): the limits at (A, A) are {0 ⪯ X ⪯ A, rank(A − X) ≤ dim ker A}, and the limiting Matsumoto fidelities at a state of rank r in dimension d form exactly [λ_{min(q,r)+1} + … + λ_r, 1] with q = d − r.

GLT counterexample (Section 6, proof and exact checks): two bounded positive definite sequences with the same symbol 1_(0,1/2] whose geometric means have symbol (4/5)·1_(0,1/2]; alternating the coupling gives means with normalised traces tending to 1/2 and 2/5 along even and odd sizes, so no eigenvalue distribution. This refutes the unrestricted symbol formula and conjecture of Ilyas, Khan, Loi and Serra-Capizzano.

Safe cases (Theorems 5 and 7, Corollaries 6 and 8, proof): closure for every Kubo–Ando mean when κ + ξ ≻ 0 a.e.; closure when κ#ξ = 0 a.e.; and always, the spectral law of the means is stochastically dominated by that of the regularised symbol κ#ξ.

Dichotomy (Theorem 9, Corollary 10, proof): for bounded Riemann-integrable scalar symbols of x only, the formula holds for every positive definite realisation if and only if |{κ + ξ = 0}| = 0 or |{κξ > 0}| = 0.

narration: When does averaging two matrices go wrong? An Evidence Press briefing. For two positive numbers, the geometric mean is the square root of their product, a kind of multiplicative midpoint. Positive definite matrices have a matching midpoint, the matrix geometric mean. It is used to average covariance matrices, to average large structured matrices, and in quantum information, where it defines a measure of how similar two quantum states are. For invertible matrices it behaves well: small changes in the inputs give small changes in the mean. But when the matrices approach singular ones, the mean can jump. This paper describes every value it can jump to, with one exact test: a block matrix built from the two inputs and the candidate value must be positive semidefinite, and its rank must be no larger than the size of the matrices. The same jump has a striking consequence. Engineers analyse huge matrices from discretised equations through a summary function called a symbol, which describes their eigenvalues. A theorem published in 2025 said that the symbol of the geometric mean is always the geometric mean of the symbols. It is not. The paper builds two sequences of matrices with identical symbols whose means have a symbol four fifths as large as predicted on half the interval, or no eigenvalue distribution at all. It also gives the repair: the shortcut is safe when the two symbols never vanish together on a region, or never overlap, and in every case the predicted symbol is an upper bound. For simple symbols that depend only on position, that is exactly the dividing line. Every result has a written proof, and a script makes over a thousand exact checks of the formulas and constructions. This is an anonymous, AI-assisted, unrefereed candidate, not peer reviewed or independently reproduced. Published on the third of November twenty twenty-six, its paper and evidence are linked from the Evidence Press release page. This briefing uses an AI-generated voice and is not additional scientific evidence.

relatedWorks.citation: Ilyas, Khan, Loi and Serra-Capizzano (2025). A maximal distribution result and numerical tests for geometric means of HPD GLT matrix-sequences with degenerate commuting/non-commuting GLT symbols. Linear Algebra and its Applications. The theorem and conjecture refuted in Section 6 (published Theorem 3 and Conjecture 1; arXiv:2505.03256 Theorem 4 and Conjecture 1).

Ahmad, Khan and Serra-Capizzano (2025). Matrix-Sequences of Geometric Means in the Case of Hidden (Asymptotic) Structures. Mathematics. The earlier restricted symbol formula, which is correct and not contradicted.
Ando (1979). Concavity of certain maps on positive definite matrices and applications to Hadamard products. Linear Algebra and its Applications. The maximal characterisation of A#B behind Theorem 1.
Pusz and Woronowicz (1975). Functional calculus for sesquilinear forms and the purification map. Reports on Mathematical Physics. Introduced the geometric mean and its maximal characterisation.
Kubo and Ando (1980). Means of positive linear operators. Mathematische Annalen. The axiomatic class of operator means used in Corollary 6.
Bhatia (2009). Positive Definite Matrices. Princeton University Press (e-book edition). Standard reference for the geometric mean and its geometry.
Garoni and Serra-Capizzano (2017). Generalized Locally Toeplitz Sequences: Theory and Applications, Vol. I. Springer. The GLT theory and Conjecture 10.1, whose status is stated conditionally.

Barbarino, Garoni and Serra-Capizzano (2020). Block generalized locally Toeplitz sequences: theory and applications in the unidimensional case. Electronic Transactions on Numerical Analysis. Source of the GLT facts used, with theorem numbers.

Barbarino, Garoni and Serra-Capizzano (2020). Block generalized locally Toeplitz sequences: theory and applications in the multidimensional case. Electronic Transactions on Numerical Analysis. Multilevel versions of the GLT facts.
Matsumoto (2018). A New Quantum Version of f-Divergence. Reality and Measurement in Algebraic Quantum Theory. The geometric (Matsumoto) fidelity studied in Corollary 3.
Moakher (2005). A Differential Geometric Approach to the Geometric Mean of Symmetric Positive-Definite Matrices. SIAM Journal on Matrix Analysis and Applications. The mean as a Riemannian midpoint.

Barachant, Bonnet, Congedo and Jutten (2012). Multiclass Brain-Computer Interface Classification by Riemannian Geometry. IEEE Transactions on Biomedical Engineering. Averaging covariance matrices in practice.
Bini, Iannazzo, Jeuris and Vandebril (2014). Geometric means of structured matrices. BIT Numerical Mathematics. Averaging structured (for example Toeplitz) matrices.

Bonnabel and Sepulchre (2009). Riemannian Metric and Geometric Mean for Positive Semidefinite Matrices of Fixed Rank. SIAM Journal on Matrix Analysis and Applications. Fixed-rank geometries built separately because the mean is not determined at the boundary.

Jones (2026). Continuity, Testing Regions and Fragility of Quantum Channel Divergences. Self-hosted preprint, section 4.12. Closest prior work: the envelope, attainability by dilation and the fidelity endpoint; credited throughout.
